backups.name: Standard Scramble
backups.fa: J.A. Juleen & party, 1912 (matches the peak's first ascent)
backups.description: A sustained Class 3-4 granite scramble above Gothic Basin's Foggy Lake to a summit with sweeping views of the Monte Cristo group, Glacier Peak, Baker, and Rainier; often paired with neighboring Gothic Peak in the same day.
hazards: steep talus and slabs
snow in the basin early season
exposure near summit
backups.overview: Del Campo Peak (6,615 ft) rises above Gothic Basin in the Morning Star Natural Resources Conservation Area, part of the classic Monte Cristo/Barlow Pass peak cluster with Gothic Peak, Morning Star, and Sperry. Reached via the Weden Creek/Gothic Basin Trail (USFS Trail #724) from Barlow Pass, it sits just above 19-acre Foggy Lake, which is fishless and often ice-covered well into summer. Above the lake the peak gives a sustained Class 3 scramble on solid, sticky granite slabs and talus, with short Class 4 moves possible if the summit gully is misread. It's commonly combined with Gothic Peak in the same long day.
backups.beta: This is the standard, easiest line up Del Campo Peak, reached via the Weden Creek/Gothic Basin trail to Foggy Lake. It is a sustained, exposed class 3-4 scramble on generally solid rock (better than much of the surrounding Cascade volcanic rock), not a roped technical climb, but the exposure and loose rock make a helmet mandatory and a fall highly consequential. The crux is route-finding: the correct entry gully off the lake and the correct line through the summit notch are both easy to get wrong, and whiteout/fog is common in the basin.
backups.turnaround: Turn back if snow slopes in the basin are hard or icy without an axe, or if the summit gully/wall area is wet or verglassed — this is a real fall-hazard scramble with sustained exposure, not a hike.
backups.permit: Northwest Forest Pass ($30 annual or $5 day-use) or a valid Interagency/America the Beautiful pass required at the Barlow Pass trailhead.
backups.descent: Reverse the scramble: downclimb the blocky face (not the gully) back to the talus/snowfield below the summit block, then descend past Foggy Lake and the Gothic Basin saddle to the Weden Creek switchbacks and the closed road back to Barlow Pass.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: From Granite Falls, Mountain Loop Highway east 31 miles to Barlow Pass; Weden Creek Trail to Gothic Basin for Del Campo Peak.
waypoints.directions: From Granite Falls, follow the Mountain Loop Highway east about 31 miles to Barlow Pass, where the pavement ends, and park at the trailhead lot at about 2,360 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required.

waypoints.name: Gothic Basin
waypoints.directions: Walk the gated Monte Cristo road about a mile to the signed junction and turn right onto Gothic Basin Trail #724. It climbs steeply through timber, fords Weden Creek, and about 3 miles from the trailhead crosses a steep avalanche gully that can hold a firm snow tongue into July, then breaks out into the meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin near 5,000 ft.

waypoints.name: Foggy Lake
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path across the basin past a small tarn and up boulder and talus slopes to Foggy Lake at about 5,200 ft, the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: Del Campo Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: Cross the boulder field on the climbers' trail along the lake's north side and climb Del Campo's south slopes to the snowfield below the summit wall near 6,200 ft. Avoid the obvious gully, which dead-ends at a vertical wall; take the blocky Class 3-4 ledges just left of it to the notch at about 6,350 ft, then turn left (west) for the short scramble to the summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: Nearly all parties do this as a long single day from the Barlow Pass trailhead: hike the Weden Creek Trail up through Gothic Basin to Foggy Lake, then scramble the blocky Class 3-4…

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful for lingering snow in the basin and on the approach switchbacks early season. Helmet strongly recommended above Foggy Lake due to rockfall from parties on the scramble.

backups.best_season: July through September; the basin and summit gullies can hold snow into early September in a heavy year (USFS Trail #724)
backups.approach: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead (~2,360 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, where the pavement ends. Walk the gated road/trail roughly 1 mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724, branching right off the old railroad grade. The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber via switchbacks, fording Weden Creek about 1 mile in (the crossing can be a wet, rock-hop affair in early season or after rain). About 1.2 miles past the creek crossing (roughly 3 miles from the trailhead), the trail crosses a steep avalanche/snow gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July — this is the trail's main hazard and can require an ice axe or careful kick-stepping in early season. Above treeline the trail breaks into subalpine meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin (~5,000 ft); tread carefully off-trail here as the meadows are fragile and use rock/gravel where possible. From the basin, follow the boot path past a small tarn and up boulder/talus slopes to Foggy Lake (~5,200 ft, about 4.7 miles from the trailhead) — the lake is a reliable water source (filter before drinking) and the last easy flat camping/staging area. From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then ascend Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward ~6,200 ft, aiming for the main summit gully. Route-finding caution: the obvious gully looks like the natural line but ends in a vertical wall — the actual route exits the gully and moves onto class 3-4 rock just left of it about 100 vertical feet below the top, working up to a notch/col at roughly 6,350 ft. From the col, turn west/left and scramble the final short pitch to the true summit (6,610-6,615 ft). Total is about 11-14 miles round trip, depending on the exact approach line, with roughly 4,200-4,300 ft of gain to the summit; snow can linger in the gully and basin into early September, and a helmet is strongly recommended for the loose upper rock.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the class 3-4 rock left of the gully back to the ~6,350 ft col, then descend the blocky wall/rock slope back into the main gully system and down the south-facing slopes to Foggy Lake. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling required — sources consistently describe it as reversing the ascent rather than a distinct technical descent line, though care is needed staying on the correct (looker's-left) rock rather than drifting into the steeper, wall-capped gully proper. Some parties note a narrow gully on the bluff above Foggy Pass (west of the true pass) that offers an alternate downclimb/traverse option back toward Foggy Lake if conditions or crowding make the standard line awkward. From Foggy Lake, retrace the boulder field and boot path back through Gothic Basin, re-cross the avalanche gully and Weden Creek, and descend Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724 back to Barlow Pass. The descent through the upper talus/scree is notably slow and knee-jarring; snow lingering in the gully or basin can actually ease the descent (plunge-stepping/glissading) in early-to-mid season but adds slip hazard if icy.
backups.bail: From anywhere on the scramble, descend back to Gothic Basin/Foggy Lake and follow the Weden Creek Trail out to Barlow Pass; from the summit block, downclimb the blocky wall (not the gully, which cliffs out) to retreat.

pitch_detail.notes: From the east side of Foggy Lake, ascend a shoulder/southwest ridge area north of the lake on heather and snow slopes.
Climb a snowfield on Del Campo's south slope, then work up left of an obvious gully (which itself cliffs out) on ledges to a notch between the South Buttress and the summit.
From just above the notch, move up the face to a second, smaller notch on the SE buttress; avoid the inviting-looking gully here and take the less-obvious scramble line beside it.
Bypass a roughly 30-ft step and scramble the final terrain to the summit on the peak's NE side.

itinerary.cal: No campfires are permitted anywhere in the Morning Star NRCA, and the Weden Creek Trail/Gothic Basin often still holds snow into July, which adds time and requires care on the final scramble; camping at Gothic Basin or Foggy Lake is a legitimate alternative to the single push if you want to split the trip into two shorter days, but it is not how most parties do it.

days.note: Nearly all parties do this as a long single day from the Barlow Pass trailhead: hike the Weden Creek Trail up through Gothic Basin to Foggy Lake, then scramble the blocky Class 3-4 face to the summit block. Most trip reports clock 6-11 hours car to car depending on pace, snow conditions, and break time.

access.rules: The trail and basin lie within the Morning Star Natural Resources Conservation Area — campfires are prohibited throughout, and visitors should stay on trail, snow, or bare rock to avoid damaging fragile heather and meadow vegetation.

climate.spring: Lingering snowpack on the approach trail and scramble into June; road/trail access depends on winter snowfall.
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window (Jul-Aug) and the most reliable time for the scramble to be free of snow and ice.
climate.winter: Mountain Loop Highway gated near Barlow Pass; area effectively inaccessible by road, deep snowpack on the peak.
climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades climate; Gothic Basin and Foggy Lake sit near 5,000 ft and hold snow into July in a normal year, longer in shaded gullies. Afternoon convective buildups are common over the exposed basin in late summer.

backups.corrections: Peak elevation was null in the provided data; filled as 6,610 ft, confirmed independently by Wikipedia, WTA, and Peakbagger.com. approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead, about 2,360 ft, where the Mountain Loop Highway pavement ends. Walk the gated road roughly a mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724, which branches right off the old railroad grade.

The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber, fording Weden Creek about a mile past the junction — a wet rock-hop in early season or after rain. Roughly 1.2 miles above the creek, and about three miles from the trailhead, the trail crosses a steep avalanche gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July. That crossing is the main hazard on the walk in.

Above treeline the trail breaks into the meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin around 5,000 ft. The meadows are fragile — travel on rock and gravel where possible. From the basin a boot path runs past a small tarn and up boulder and talus slopes to Foggy Lake at about 5,200 ft, roughly 4.7 miles in. The lake is the last reliable water and the last flat staging or camping ground.

From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on the climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then work up Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward the permanent snowfield below the summit walls at roughly 6,200 ft.

hazards: Steep snow tongue where the trail crosses the avalanche gully, into July

approach_variants.baseFinding: At the top of the snowfield you face a rock wall with one obvious gully splitting it. The obvious gully is the wrong line: it looks like the natural way, and it steepens and ends against a vertical wall about a hundred vertical feet below the top. The correct start is the blocky, staircase-like class 3-4 ledge system immediately to climber's left of that gully. It carries a boot path — if there is a bootpath under your feet you are on it, if you are on clean untracked rock in a narrowing groove you are not. The ledges lead to a notch on the southeast ridge at about 6,350 ft; from the notch turn left (west) for the last short scramble to the true summit at 6,610 ft. If the ground you are on constricts into a chimney and turns class 4 near its top, you are in the gully — reverse and move left onto the ledges. Parties who scramble directly to the notch on 4th class have simply missed the class 3 ledges a little further left.

A helmet is strongly recommended for the loose upper rock.

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.notes: The usual camp for Gothic Peak and Del Campo Peak, at the top of the Gothic Basin trail beneath both summits. The basin is fragile, so keep off the meadows and heather.
bivy.permit: No permit required; no campfires; camp only on rock or established sites
bivy.capacity: A few established sites, mostly on rock and bare ground near the south shore; space is tight on summer weekends

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For Gothic Peak this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for Del Campo it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. Treat the provenance of this water seriously: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land outside designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. Campfires are prohibited throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

backups.overview: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.
backups.beta: Rather than the popular Scatter Lake approach, this line reaches Abernathy from Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing a spur ridge from a small tarn onto the main north ridge, then scrambling the crest — weaving around or over gendarmes — to the top. Route-finding is loose and 'pick-your-own-adventure' in spots; parties report it as noticeably harder and slower than the standard route.
backups.turnaround: Loose rock, exposed class 3-4 steps, and a long, largely trail-less descent mean parties should set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight for a slower-than-expected reverse scramble, especially in poor visibility or if unfamiliar with route-finding on open ridges.
backups.rappels: None — unroped scramble; no rappels reported by parties ascending or descending.
backups.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or camp in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No parking pass is needed at the Wolf Creek trailhead.
obj_haz: route-finding on an unmarked spur ridge

waypoints.name: Wolf Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of Wolf Creek Trail #527, at the end of a gravel Forest Service road west of Winthrop.
waypoints.directions: From Winthrop, take SR 20 across the Methow River bridge at the south end of town and turn right onto Twin Lakes Road. In about 1.5 miles turn right onto Wolf Creek Road, then follow the signs onto gravel Forest Service road to the Wolf Creek Trailhead at about 2,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Gardner Meadows
waypoints.note: End of the Wolf Creek Trail, about 10 miles in, and the usual camp. From the last campsites a faint path crosses Wolf Creek toward Abernathy Lake and the upper tarn. Not plotted on the map.
waypoints.directions: Follow Wolf Creek Trail #527 up the Wolf Creek valley about 10 miles to its end at Gardner Meadows. The trail drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek right away, then rolls up and down through burned forest, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on.

waypoints.name: North Ridge saddle
waypoints.note: Saddle on the north ridge crest roughly 0.6 mi north of the summit. The coordinate is an estimate, not a surveyed fix.
waypoints.directions: From the last campsites, cross Wolf Creek on a faint path toward Abernathy Lake; it soon fades into old burn and deadfall. Stay high above the lake and make a rising traverse into the upper basin to the small tarn with cabin remains, where the stream just below is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge to the north ridge crest, with a few exposed class 3 moves.

waypoints.name: Abernathy Peak summit
waypoints.note: High point of Abernathy Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow a short boot path south along the crest past old mining cables and equipment. Where it fades, scramble class 2-3 boulders and scree on or near the crest to the summit.

backups.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. The non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a tarn and a spur ridge onto the crest, then a choose-your-own-line scramble along the ridge crest with a few class 3 moves on a spur ridge. Parties do not place cams or nuts or use a rope.
what_to_bring: helmet (loose rock/rockfall risk on talus and scree)
trekking poles for scree and talus
ice axe and/or microspikes if snow lingers near the tarn or on the spur ridge (common into early summer on this east-side, north-facing approach)

backups.pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
backups.approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.
backups.descent_text: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back toward the top of the spur ridge (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From there, most parties drop down the scree slope toward the tarn with the old mining camp rather than reversing the spur ridge; an old path leaves the crest and descends to the upper lake. From the tarn, retrace the rough off-trail line past Abernathy Lake back to Gardner Meadows and follow the Wolf Creek Trail out to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
backups.bail: Retreat down the ridge to the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Ridge-crest scramble from the top of the spur ridge to the summit, weaving around or over gendarmes; loose rock and unmarked route-finding.

itinerary.cal: The ridge and the slopes above the tarn can hold snow into early summer; most parties climb it July-October.

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
approach_variants.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
approach_variants.baseFinding: The dried-up tarn with cabin remnants is the proof, and the old mine on the crest confirms it. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.

backups.overview: The Gerdine Ridge and Cool Glacier route climbs Glacier Peak's south side, typically via the White Pass and Glacier Gap. It is a popular alternative to the Sitkum, often combined with a scenic high traverse beneath the peak.
backups.beta: From Glacier Gap (7,300 ft), ascend northward, initially contouring the left slope below Glacier Gap Peak (7,739 ft), then regain the ridge and continue to about 8,400 ft. Traverse NE onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, then ascend the Cool Glacier westward until regaining the ridge at its top, finishing to the summit. A variant stays on the nose of the cleaver where the standard line steps onto the glacier near 8,500-8,600 ft, following a climbers' path when melted out up mostly Class 3-4 ground with a few low fifth-class moves over Disappointment Peak (9,755 ft), then drops about 150 ft to the saddle above the Cool Glacier to rejoin the standard route. It avoids most of the glacier travel and crevasse hazard in exchange for sustained loose, rockfall-prone scrambling.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before the summit push and hold to it — rockfall below Disappointment Peak and softening snow bridges both worsen as the day warms.

waypoints.name: Foam Creek Trail / ridge saddle crossing
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT on the Foam Creek climbers' path and cross the ridge saddle into the White Chuck Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: From the PCT at White Pass, take the Foam Creek climbers' trail east for about two miles, then cross the ridge at a saddle on its north side near 6,600 ft. This saddle is the end of trail travel — beyond it the route is open basin and snow.

waypoints.name: White Chuck Glacier basin crossing
waypoints.note: Open glacial basin traverse trending NE toward Glacier Gap; rope up here as crevasses can be present even though the grade is gentle.
waypoints.directions: Drop north off the saddle into the open White Chuck Glacier basin and trend northeast across it. The grade is gentle, but it is glacier under the snow, so rope up before you start across rather than partway.

waypoints.name: Glacier Gap
waypoints.note: Large, popular camp area with many established sites on a broad gap; standard base camp for the Gerdine Ridge/Cool Glacier route.
waypoints.directions: Continue northeast across the basin, gaining a few hundred feet to the broad gap where the White Chuck and Suiattle glaciers meet. Established sites are spread across the gap, and it is the last flat ground before the summit push.

waypoints.name: Cool Glacier saddle (Gerdine-Cool col)
waypoints.note: Saddle between Disappointment Peak and Glacier Peak where the Gerdine Ridge route tops out onto the Cool Glacier for the final push.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp on crampons, losing a little height onto rocky Gerdine Ridge, then climb north, contouring the slope below Glacier Gap Peak before regaining the crest and following it to roughly 8,400 ft. The climber's track ends near a gendarme around 8,500 ft — rope up there, traverse northeast onto the Gerdine and upper Suiattle ice, and end-run one or two crevasses where it bends into the Cool Glacier. Keep moving on that traverse; the cliffs of Disappointment Peak above it shed rock. Finish by climbing west up the Cool Glacier to regain the ridge at the saddle.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Glacier Peak (Dakobed); broad volcanic summit with views across the North Cascades.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the glacier travel is over. Rejoin the climber's trail and finish up one short, steep pitch of pumice and broken volcanic rock to the top — unroped class 2-3, with no rock gear needed.

backups.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,050 ft, off FR 49/Sloan Creek Road), hike ~9 mi to White Pass on the PCT. Continue east on the Foam Creek Trail ~2 mi, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, then traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending NE to Glacier Gap (~7,300 ft), the standard high camp where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet. Summit day is roughly 7 mi round trip with about 3,450 ft of gain, some of it height lost and regained along the way: climb gentle snow above camp, follow a climber's track on volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers, end-run a crevasse or two, then rejoin the climber's trail for the final steep pitch to the summit.
backups.descent_text: No rappelling; reverse the ascent line on foot. From the summit, descend the ridge to the 9,600 ft col, then down the Cool Glacier to the 9,100 ft col. On the traverse back beneath Disappointment Peak, keep lower and farther from the face than on the way in to cut the time spent under its rockfall. Crevasses on the Cool Glacier open wider as summer goes on and snow bridges weaken, so stay roped and probe suspect bridges. From Glacier Gap, return across the White Chuck basin to White Pass and out the North Fork Sauk River Trail.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then the Foam Creek high traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, take Trail #649 up the valley and then the steep switchbacks to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, roughly nine miles in.

Rather than dropping into the basin, continue east on the Foam Creek trail for about two miles, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, and traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending north-east to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft — where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet, and the standard high camp.

Summit day from Glacier Gap is short in distance but has intermediate descent in it as well as gain: gentle snow above camp, then a climbers' track over volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.
hazards: rockfall corridor below Disappointment Peak on the traverse
crevasses on the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
loose volcanic scree on the connecting ground
long approach with no maintained trail above White Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is confirmed the same way as for the cleaver — it is the col where two glaciers meet, not a saddle with ice on one side only.

This route deliberately avoids the fourth-class ground: the line skirts Disappointment Peak by staying on the upper edges of the Gerdine and then the Cool. So the test that you are on the right variation is that you are on snow and scree the whole way, working around the peak rather than over it. If you are scrambling rock and gaining a summit, you have drifted onto the direct line over Disappointment Peak.

On the Cool Glacier expect to end-run one or two crevasses before rejoining the climbers' track for the final steep pitch to the summit — that track, worn into scree and snow by traffic, is the most reliable confirmation you are on the standard line, so look for it rather than for a feature.

climbing_route.label: Gentle snow above Glacier Gap camp
climbing_route.notes: From the ~7,300 ft Glacier Gap camp head north, sidehilling first on the left slope and then on the right slope below Glacier Gap Peak (7,739 ft), then regain the ridge and follow it to about 8,400 ft. A short scramble of about 15 ft at the top of this section drops onto the glacier.

climbing_route.label: Volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
climbing_route.notes: Traverse northeast onto the upper Suiattle and Gerdine glacier ice, passing below and right of the cliffs of Disappointment Peak. Few crevasses, but rockfall off that face is frequent and can include very large blocks, worst after about 10 AM — keep a wide berth and do not stop beneath it. Late in the season a short stretch of bare ice appears.

climbing_route.label: Cool Glacier to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: At about 9,200 ft the ice bends sharply left onto the Cool Glacier; climb it westward to the saddle between Disappointment Peak and the main peak at the glacier's top. This is where the real crevasses are — small cracks at the bend, then snow bridges and crevasse hops that deteriorate fast in late summer — so stay roped.

climbing_route.label: Final steep pitch to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge north on the climbers' trail, up loose pumice and scree that slides back underfoot, to about 10,000 ft, then climb steep snow or loose rock for the last ~500 ft to the 10,541 ft summit, which sits on the west side of the top. Which surface you get depends on the season.

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
bivy.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

backups.name: Standard Scramble
backups.season: Jun-Oct for dry scrambling; climbable in winter/spring with an ice axe, crampons, and often a rope for the summit gully
hazards: Short, steep, exposed 4th class gully near the summit — loose rock, often wet/muddy, the main technical crux
Dense brush (slide alder, devil's club) on the lower approach off-trail sections
Cornices and avalanche terrain in and above the summit gully during winter/spring ascents
Unreliable/changing road-gate status on Olney Creek Road, which can add unplanned miles and elevation gain to the day
Inaccurate mapped road alignment near Olney Creek — parties note the drawn road doesn't match the road on the ground
backups.overview: Mount Stickney (5,307 ft) sits on the ridge dividing the Sultan Basin from the Skykomish Valley near Index and Gold Bar, within the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest's Wild Sky Wilderness. It's a prominent, easily-recognized peak from US-2 eastbound but a deceptively involved outing: roughly 12-13 miles round trip with about 3,500 ft of gain, most of it on old logging road and a faint climbers' path through heavy brush before a short, steep, exposed gully leads to the summit ridge and plateau. Named for a prospector who worked claims in the area (it was earlier called Prospect Mountain).
backups.beta: From the end of the drivable Sultan Basin/Olney Creek Road, follow the old roadbed and then a boot path up the NW ridge. The path fades around 4,200 ft; from there, navigate cross-country southeast past a small pond near Point 4875, over a second ridge crest, then traverse an open slope south/southeast into Stickney's rocky summit basin. Scramble talus and dirt up to the summit ridge, follow it east across a small plateau, then cross a short but genuinely exposed section of ridge to the true summit. In winter and spring a snow gully below the summit ridge is often climbed instead, and many parties rope up for it.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, largely unmarked approach and a summit ridge that becomes more exposed in poor visibility or snow, set a firm turnaround time that guarantees the party is off the exposed ridge and back on the marked boot path well before dark or before weather deteriorates.
backups.rappels: 0-1, conditions- and party-dependent. In dry conditions most parties downclimb the summit gully (easy 4th class on dirt and rock). When it is wet, muddy or the party would rather not downclimb exposed 4th class, one short rappel of roughly 50-60 ft gets past the steepest section. Anchors are natural — slings around trees or horns, including one reported around a mountain hemlock — so carry your own webbing and rap rings and back up any tat you find.
backups.descent: Reverse the scramble and brushy approach.
obj_haz: Loose talus and scree in the summit basin
Route-finding across a fading boot path and overgrown old logging road
Short but genuinely exposed ridge crossing just below the true summit
Snow/ice-filled gully below the summit ridge in winter and spring
Gated access road adding several miles of extra walking each way

waypoints.name: Olney Creek Road Gate
waypoints.note: Gated logging-road junction on Sultan Basin Road ~11.2-11.5 mi north of Sultan; no formal lot, park on the road shoulder.
waypoints.directions: From Sultan, follow Sultan Basin Road north about 11.2 to 11.5 miles to the gated junction with Olney Creek Road. Olney Creek Road is closed to public vehicle travel, so that gate is where the drive ends. There is no formal lot — park on the road shoulder at the junction. The day starts on foot from the gate, walking the closed logging road uphill.

waypoints.name: Second Switchback / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Closed Olney Creek logging road levels off at the second switchback here; a boot path breaks off to the right and follows the ridge crest toward the summit.
waypoints.directions: Walk the closed Olney Creek logging road uphill about 2.25 miles, past a first switchback, to a second switchback where the grade eases around 3,700 ft. Nothing is signed here and mapped road alignments are unreliable, so go by the switchback on the ground.

waypoints.name: Ridge Path Fade-Out
waypoints.note: The climbers' path peters out on the ridge crest around 4,000-4,200 ft; leave it and traverse cross-country southeast toward One Acre Lake.
waypoints.directions: Leave the road on the unsigned but well-established boot path on the right (north) side, which climbs onto a forested ridge crest and follows it until the tread fades out around 4,050 to 4,200 ft.

waypoints.name: One Acre Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake passed on its east side; last reliable water before the dry summit basin, but no confirmed shoreline coordinate found.
waypoints.directions: Leave the tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake.

waypoints.name: Upper Drainage Tarns
waypoints.note: Ascend the drainage above the lake to a cluster of small tarns; flattish ground here works as a rough bivy for an overnight attempt.
waypoints.directions: Pass the lake on its east side and follow the drainage above it up to a cluster of small tarns around 4,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Summit Basin Gully
waypoints.note: Rocky basin/boulder field below the final ridge; the gully to the summit crest is wet, muddy, easy 4th class and can hold old snow or cornice debris into early summer — many parties carry a rope to rappel it.
waypoints.directions: Work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block, into the rocky basin and boulder field below it. The gully to take is the one on the right, immediately west of the summit hump; in winter and spring at least one avalanche-prone slope is crossed on the way.

waypoints.name: Mount Stickney Summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a short, airy walk/scoot across an exposed ridge section past a small plateau to the final rock hump.
waypoints.directions: Climb the wet, loose, easy fourth-class gully to the notch just under the summit ridge, then walk and scoot across the short, exposed ridge past a small plateau to the final rock hump.

what_to_bring: Ice axe and crampons for winter/spring ascents when the gully is snow or ice-filled
A 30 m rope and basic rappel gear — useful even in summer for the crux gully, where informal rappel anchors exist near the top
Sturdy boots and gaiters for brush and mud on the lower approach
A GPS track from a recent trip report rather than relying solely on the mapped road line near Olney Creek
Bug spray — brushy, buggy approach in summer
pro_tips: Carry a rope even for a summer scramble attempt — the crux gully is loose 4th class and often wet, and roughly three informal rappel stations near its top get used regularly for the descent.
Don't trust the mapped road line near Olney Creek Road; several parties note it doesn't match the actual roadbed, and the gate position itself has moved closer to Sultan Basin Road in recent years.
Leave the old roadbed for the climbers' path only after it levels out (around 3,700 ft) and expect the path itself to fade around 4,000-4,200 ft, after which it's cross-country past One Acre Lake.
watch_out: The summit gully being wet or muddy even in dry summer conditions — many parties rope up here, especially for the descent
Cornices overhanging the summit area in winter and spring that look like solid ground
Losing the faint climbers' path around 4,000-4,200 ft and having to navigate cross-country past One Acre Lake by dead reckoning/GPS
Road-gate position changing year to year, turning an expected drive into a multi-mile road walk
backups.pro_needs: The summer NW Ridge route needs no rock protection — it's an unroped scramble over talus, dirt, and one short exposed ridge crest. In winter and spring, carry an ice axe and crampons; some parties rope up or fix a hand line on the snow gully below the summit ridge.
backups.best_season: July through September is the reliable window once the summit gully has melted out and lower brush has died back somewhat; the gully can hold snow/ice well into June and refreezes with the first fall storms in October-November. The peak is also a locally popular low-elevation winter/spring snow climb when the approach roads are snow-covered and the gully is filled in, though parties then rope up for the steep final pitch and manage cornice/avalanche hazard.
backups.approach: From the gate on Olney Creek Road (the drive-in ends here, at roughly 1,700 ft, since the road has been closed to public vehicle travel), the route starts as a road-walk. Follow the closed logging road uphill for about 2.25 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second switchback where the grade eases around 3,700 ft — this is the key junction. Leave the road here and pick up an unsigned but well-established climbers' path on the right (north) side, which climbs onto and follows a forest ridge crest. The path fades out around 4,050-4,200 ft; from that point, leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge. Cross open slopes on this ridge into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake (roughly 6 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the road gate/Sultan Basin Road) — this is the last reliable water source and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the lake, work up and around toward the base of the prominent summit block, aiming for the bowl directly below it. The final approach pitch is a steep slope/gully leading to the notch just below the summit ridge; expect a mix of dirt, talus, and (in early season) snow, with the gully becoming genuinely difficult — muddy, loose, and exposed — once it melts out in mid-to-late summer. Route-finding through the mid-mountain traverse (road-walk to ridge path to cross-country bench) is the crux of the approach itself and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit; the mapped road alignment is reportedly inaccurate here, so trust the on-the-ground second-switchback landmark over the map. Winter and spring ascents cross at least one avalanche-prone slope below the summit bowl — one trip report noted watching roughly 20 slides release nearby during a single outing, so avoid this line in or after a storm cycle or during rapid warming.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: back across the short exposed ridge section from the summit hump, then down through the notch and back into the steep summit gully. In dry, snow-free conditions most parties downclimb the gully directly (it's an easy-4th-class scramble on dirt and rock), then reverse the cross-country traverse past the pond near point 4875 back to the climbers' path, and follow that path and the closed road back down to the gate. This is a walk-off/downclimb for competent scramblers in good conditions — no rappelling is strictly required. That said, the gully is frequently wet, muddy, and loose, and parties uncomfortable downclimbing exposed 4th class on that surface commonly opt to rappel it instead; there are at least a few natural anchor options (slings around trees/rock horns, including one built around a mountain hemlock) near the top of the gully, consistent with a single short rappel of roughly 50-60 feet to get past the steepest, most exposed section — a single 30m/60m rope is more than sufficient either doubled or as a single strand. These are backcountry natural anchors, not bolted or fixed hardware, so carry your own webbing/cord and rap rings, and back up any tat you find before trusting it. In winter conditions, most parties rope up for the gully on the way down (not just up) given the exposure, and cornices can form along the summit ridge — the guidance from trip reports is to stay climbers' right on the ridge and rig a hand line if anyone in the party is uncomfortable, since cornices can look like solid ground but are not. Below the gully, the descent hazards mirror the approach: avalanche exposure on the summit bowl slopes in winter/spring, and easy-to-lose route-finding through the unmarked ridge-path-to-road transition around 3,700-4,200 ft, especially in whiteout or at dusk.
backups.bail: Descend the ascent route; bailing is complicated by the brush and terrain.

itinerary.cal: Best done mid-to-late summer after the crux gully and boulder field lose snow; earlier-season attempts commonly get turned back by avalanche-prone snow slopes on the traverses.

days.note: A long, strenuous single-day scramble on Sultan Basin/Olney Creek Road: a gated logging-road walk gives way to a brushy, unmaintained boot path, a rising traverse past One Acre Lake, a boulder field, and a short exposed gully/ridge scramble to the summit. Route-finding is the crux as much as the terrain — several parties turn back in early-season snow or after missing the unmarked turn off the road.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass: $5 for a day pass or $30 for an annual pass, available at ranger stations, REI, or online.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness Act regulations apply within the Wild Sky Wilderness boundary: groups of 12 or fewer, no motorized or mechanized (including bike) travel once inside the wilderness boundary, Leave No Trace practices.
access.permit: No wilderness entry permit or self-issue system is required for Wild Sky Wilderness. A parking pass (Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency pass) is generally expected at Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF trailheads.
access.closures: The Olney Creek Road gate location has moved over the years — near mile 10-11 from the highway as of 2009, but in the 2020s parties describe it closed much closer to the Sultan Basin Road junction. Treat any specific older driving mileage as unreliable and check current conditions first.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Skykomish Ranger District — Wild Sky Wilderness (designated 2008).
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

overnight_permit.where: Sign the trailhead register if one is present; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the trailhead.

road.name: Sultan Basin Road to Olney Creek Road (FS spur)
road.status: Sultan Basin Road is paved/good gravel; the Olney Creek spur is an old logging road now gated and closed to vehicles at a point that has varied by year.
road.driveNote: High-clearance was historically useful for the final stretch of Olney Creek Road when it was open to that point; today plan on walking or biking a closed roadbed for several miles regardless of vehicle.
road.seasonalGate: Gate position is not fixed year to year — confirm current status with the Skykomish Ranger District before planning driving mileage.

climate.typical: A wet, brushy western Cascades foothill peak — at only 5,307 ft the trailhead and lower approach see rain more than snow much of the year, but the shaded summit gully and upper basin can hold snow and ice into June and refill with the season's first storms in October-November.

bySeason.fall: Good conditions typically hold into October until the rains return; shorter daylight means an earlier start.
bySeason.spring: Lingering snow in the gully and upper basin commonly persists into June; underlying rock/mud can be wet and slick where snow has thinned.
bySeason.summer: The reliable window (roughly July-September): gully is snow-free but still loose and often muddy/slick in the 4th class section; brush on the lower approach is fully leafed out.
bySeason.winter: A locally popular low-elevation snow climb; expect to boot-pack or kick steps up the summit gully and to rope up for it, plus manage cornice and avalanche hazard on the upper mountain — check the NWAC Stevens Pass forecast beforehand.

approach_variants.name: Olney Creek Road gate, the closed logging road and One Acre Lake
approach_variants.notes: The drive ends at the gate where Olney Creek Road leaves the Sultan Basin Road, and the day starts on foot up the closed roadbed. Walk the road uphill for a little over two miles, past a first switchback and on to a second one where the grade noticeably eases around 3,700 ft — that second switchback is the key junction and there is nothing signed about it. Mapped road alignments in this area are known to be wrong, so trust the switchback you can see on the ground over the line drawn on a map. Leave the road there and pick up an unsigned but well-established boot path on the right, north side, which climbs onto a forest ridge crest and follows it. The path fades out somewhere around 4,050 to 4,200 ft; from there leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake. Pass the lake on its east side, follow the drainage above it to a cluster of small tarns, and then work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block. This mid-mountain sequence — road to ridge path to cross-country bench — is the crux of the walk-in and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit.
approach_variants.season: July through September once the gully has melted out and the lower brush has died back. The gully holds snow and ice into June, and it refreezes with the first fall storms. It is also climbed as a snow route in winter and spring, when parties rope up for the final pitch and manage cornice and avalanche hazard.
hazards: a short, steep, exposed fourth-class gully near the summit — loose, often wet and muddy, and the real crux
at least one avalanche-prone slope below the summit bowl in winter and spring
cornices along the summit ridge that can look like solid ground
dense slide alder and devil's club on the lower off-trail sections
an unreliable gate status on the access road that can add unplanned miles
mapped road alignments that do not match the road on the ground
approach_variants.baseFinding: Take the gully on the right, the one that tops out just west of the summit. From the rocky basin and boulder field beneath the summit block, more than one weakness leads toward the crest. The correct one is the gully to the right, immediately west of the summit hump, and it runs to the notch just under the summit ridge. Its condition is the second identifier and it is not a pleasant one: this gully is characteristically wet, muddy and loose, easy fourth class on dirt and rock rather than clean stone, and it becomes noticeably harder once the snow that fills it in winter and spring has melted out. Near the top of it are natural anchor options — slings around trees and rock horns, including one built around a mountain hemlock — because parties who dislike downclimbing it rappel roughly fifty to sixty feet past the steepest section. If the gully you are in tops out anywhere other than the crest immediately west of the summit hump, it is the wrong one. Above the notch, the ridge runs east across a small plateau and then a short, genuinely airy section to the final rock hump; stay climbers' right through the difficult bits and rig a hand line if anyone is uneasy, since cornices along this crest look solid and are not.

climbing_route.label: Bowl below the summit block
climbing_route.notes: From One Acre Lake work up and around to the base of the prominent summit block, aiming for the bowl directly beneath it. In winter and spring at least one avalanche-prone slope below this bowl must be crossed — one party reported watching roughly 20 slides release nearby in a single outing, so avoid the line during or after a storm cycle and in rapid warming.

climbing_route.label: Steep gully to the notch below the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: A steep slope/gully leads from the bowl to the notch just under the summit ridge: dirt, talus, and snow in early season. Once it melts out in mid-to-late summer the gully turns genuinely difficult — muddy, loose and exposed.

bivy.name: One Acre Lake, under Mount Stickney
bivy.notes: The one place worth camping on Mount Stickney, and the reason the peak is doable at all now that the road is gated low. The route leaves the Sultan Basin road onto the old Olney Creek logging road, which used to let a high-clearance vehicle grind up to around 2,100 feet and is now closed at its very beginning, so the road walk is five to six miles before any climbing starts. Where the road levels near 3,700 feet a trail cuts off to the right along a ridge; leave that around 4,050 feet and traverse southeast to the lake. From camp the route continues southeast past a set of tarns near 4,500 feet, up to about 4,800, and then traverses into the boulder basin below the summit, taking a gully just west of the top to gain the crest. This is a winter and early spring peak by preference, not a summer one: the low western start means it comes into condition when everything else is buried, and deep snow covers a boulder field that is loose, awkward and slow when bare. The trade is that the same snow brings real avalanche exposure on the traverses above the lake, and early-season parties have found route-finding and slope assessment to be the hard part rather than the climbing. Expect a long day either way, and expect the road walk to feel longer on the way out.
bivy.water: The lake, and snowmelt in the drainages above it well into July. Treat everything; the basin is shallow and the water warms.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is outside the Wild Sky boundary on a mix of state and federal land. No pass at the gated roadhead. Fires are a poor idea in a basin this small and are restricted through most summers.
bivy.capacity: A few flat spots on the benches around a small tarn, informal and unimproved. Two or three tents.

bivy.name: Sultan Basin road pullouts and the Olney Creek gate
bivy.notes: A pure staging pullout for Mount Stickney, included because the road walk is now long enough that starting it at first light matters. From US 2 in Sultan, the Sultan Basin road runs north for roughly eleven and a half miles before the Olney Creek road turns off on the right, and the gate is at the very start of that turn. Sleeping at the gate saves an hour of driving in the dark and puts the five-to-six mile approach march in the coolest part of the morning. The Sultan Basin road is paved for its lower miles and gravel above; it is generally drivable in a normal car to the gate, but conditions after a wet winter are worth checking. This is working forest and watershed land rather than recreation land, so expect industrial traffic, expect gates to move, and do not count on a pullout being available where it was last year. There is no established camping anywhere between here and One Acre Lake.
bivy.water: Olney Creek, a short way along the closed road, where a spur drops to a bridge and a gravel bar. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Mixed state and municipal watershed land, with day-use restrictions posted in places and gates that change. Read the signs at the gate rather than assuming dispersed camping is permitted where you have parked. Fire restrictions here are usually stricter than on national forest and are enforced.
bivy.capacity: Gravel pullouts and a turnaround at the gate. Room to sleep in or beside a vehicle, nothing more. No toilet, no table, no fire ring you should trust.

backups.overview: The Southwest Buttress is Dorado Needle's longest and most sustained rock route: over 1,000 ft (9 pitches) of quality granite up steep cracks and slabs, past photogenic gendarmes, to an airy knife-edge summit ridge. Rated Grade III, 5.8, it's a popular objective in its own right, reached via the same Eldorado-area glacier approach used for Eldorado Peak and the East Ridge.
backups.beta: A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit, reached via a long glaciated approach from the Eldorado trailhead.
backups.turnaround: Given the length (9-13 pitches) and afternoon-thunderstorm-prone terrain, set an early turnaround time and account for the moat crossing at the base, which becomes more dangerous as the season progresses.
backups.rappels: Rappel from gully top, or double-rope rappel from fixed ring/sling on summit ridge to the NW Ridge snow section.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Eldorado/Marble Creek glaciated cirque; carry a satellite communicator.
backups.descent: Either rappel down the approach gully (single rope), or from a large boulder about 10m north of the true summit — which has a fixed rappel ring and sling — make one double-rope rappel.
obj_haz: Moat crossing at the base (roped crossing recommended)

The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.

backups.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams to #3 Camalot (rarely need the #3) with doubles in 0.5, 0.75, and 1 inch, plus a set of nuts; natural gear anchors are used throughout — no fixed anchors on route except the rappel station near the summit.

Pitch 1 trends right about 55-57m (5.6, one 5.7/5.8 move) to a cam anchor; higher up, the cleanest line follows a left-leaning, right-facing corner with good cracks for roughly 90m before blockier terrain leads to the summit ridge.

backups.pro_needs: Good crack systems take cams well throughout; doubles in the 0.5-1" range cover most placements.
backups.best_season: Late July through August, based on typical trip-report dates; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps with the glacier travel but requires crampons on the gully.
backups.approach: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. Where the Southwest Buttress approach diverges is the final glacier traverse: from camp, continue across the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister Glacier, heading toward the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The base of the Southwest Buttress is reached via a prominent gully - often snow-filled year-round - that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side. The recorded round-trip distance is about 25.75 km, somewhat longer than the East Ridge approach because the SW start point is farther along the glacier traverse.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to a large rock/boulder on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, where a fixed rappel ring and sling (recently reported as reinforced with an additional sling) anchors the route's single rappel: a double-rope rappel (both strands, ~60m rope) that lowers you to a steep snow slope which, in normal-season conditions, keeps a solid connection to the rock, so a moat crossing usually isn't required at this point. From the bottom of that rappel, downclimb/glissade the snow slope to the notch at the base of the route - the same notch used on the approach - and reverse the glacier travel back toward camp. Some parties describe an alternate single-rope-length rappel off the top of the summit gully instead of the ridge-boulder station; functionally this is still a one-rappel descent, just from a slightly different anchor. Either way, plan on exactly one rope-length transition, not a multi-pitch rappel sequence - the rest of the descent is downclimbing, scrambling, and glacier travel. Because this is a moderate Grade III+ route rather than a big-wall-style descent, no v-thread or chained-rappel sequence is needed in summer conditions; the main descent hazard is the moat at the base of the route staying open or widening late in the season, which can complicate reconnecting with the glacier.
backups.bail: Multiple fixed rappel anchors exist along the buttress and near the summit ridge; retreat is generally feasible by rappelling the line of ascent or reversing to the gully.

pitch_detail.notes: A full rope-length up a corner then slightly right; mostly 5.6 climbing with one committing 5.7/5.8 move near the top. Build the anchor on gear (cams to 3 inches) in a crack.
Continue up and right to a small plateau; the belay is built on 0.5-1 inch cams or a few nut placements.
A short class-4 gully scramble gives way to a rising traverse up and left to a comfortable ledge; belay on 1-2 inch cam and nut placements.
A half-rope-length pitch trending left to gain the ridge crest — staying left is important, since climbing right leads into an unwanted 5.10 overhang.

The route's variation crux: a sustained corner past sections of loose rock with limited protection, per multiple trip reports. The standard (non-variation) line instead follows easier low-5th-class ridge scrambling to the same flat shelf.
Climb a right-leaning crack, then continue straight up a wall on good holds; belay off gear near the top of the ridge.
Follow the ridge crest, then traverse left to a wide crack between slabs; the belay is a sling backed up in a notch.
Choose between a loose gully with a chockstone or a rightward line up the wall toward the summit-ridge crack; both options top out near the same point below the final ridge.
A short final traverse along the summit ridge — the same terrain shared with the upper Northwest Ridge — leads to the narrow, exposed high point.

June.reason: Deep snow covers the Eldorado talus and glaciers, which speeds travel, but the buttress ledges still hold snow and the approach slopes carry avalanche risk.

August.reason: Rock on the buttress is dry and the approach gully usually still holds firm snow for crampons, making the glacier crossing and the climb both straightforward.
